title: Optimizely confirms massive cyberattack on customer websites injected stealer malware
summary: Attackers apparently from China used an authentication security hole within the popular Optimizely AI platform for marketers to steal from at least 178 sites owned by some of the planet’s largest companies. Named victims featured vendors including Zoom, Paychex, Equifax, and GitLab, and end-user enterprises including Starbucks, IKEA, Mattel, American Eagle, Air France, Mutual of Omaha, Heineken, Home Chef, Cinnabon, American Eagle, Levi, Costco and HSBC. Salesforce issued a statement confirming that it had also been impacted by the attack. “Salesforce is investigating unauthorized modifications to scripts provided by Optimizely and used on certain Salesforce websites,” it wrote in an email statement. “As a precaution, Salesforce is confirming that Optimizely scripts are disabled across preview and production instances.” The attacks were discovered by UK-based security researcher Scott Helme , the founder of Report URI, who said in an interview that his team had confirmed 178 victims, but that there could be more. “That’s the number that we directly observed and that all carried the same infection,” he said. Helme published a report about the attacks on Monday, in which he described an attack methodology where an Optimizely capability in its Web Experimentation product facilitating adding members to a site’s development team was leveraged to insert malware into the sites. “The malware was a multi-purpose kit. It swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker’s, skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and on iPhones and iPads it delivered the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits,” Helme wrote. “The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy. A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.” Optimizely customers load a JavaScript “snippet” from Optimizely’s CDN onto their sites which contains Optimizely code, the customer’s A/B tests

title: When does cooling an AI processor from inside the silicon improve efficiency?
summary: Engineers can now etch cooling channels into the back of an AI processor and circulate liquid close to its hottest regions. Tests on a working CPU and an NVIDIA GH200 show what this changes for sustained clock speed, GPU temperature and nearby high-bandwidth memory. The electricity question requires a wider view. A retrofit at Lawrence Livermore reveals how much depends on which fans slow down and where the heat finally goes. A separate Berkeley Lab study shows how changing the cooling plant alters the projected savings. Together these results explain when a data centre might serve more AI requests within an existing power limit, which parts of a liquid-cooled rack it could reuse, and what manufacturers must establish about sealed channels, filtration and reliability before deploying the technology across a fleet.

title: ‘Human’ wins Cambridge dictionary’s word of the year
summary: Meaning and use of word has become more important in age of AI chatbot, says dictionary In a world where the line between people and machines is more blurred than ever, Cambridge dictionary has sided with natural intelligence for its word of the year: human. Breakthroughs in artificial intelligence – led by the arrival of ChatGPT three years ago – have made the question of what it means to be human as vexed as ever, but the dictionary has drawn a firm line with its choice of the word of 2026, defining “human” as “having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines”.
